newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Inflation, escudo worry prevented Portugal rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Inflation, escudo worry prevented Portugal rate cut.

text.p: The Bank of Portugal's decision to leave its key rate unchanged showed that it is not prepared to ease policy at a moment of escudo weakness as well as that it may be more concerned about inflation than was thought earlier, analysts said.

The bank defied analysts' predictions for an up to 50 basis points cut in the key draining rate, leaving it intact at 6.2 percent on Friday when announcing terms for the next commercial bank reserve period.
Some analysts said that the bank might be signalling that it would not be moving the rates until after the January inflation figures were known early in February.

"There are two elements: one is the fact that the escudo has slipped and the other is concern over the January inflation number," said Rui Martins dos Santos, chief economist at Banco Portugues de Investimento (BPI).

"The Bank has said it is not ready to cut if the escudo is not stable and as long as it is not absolutely certain about the favourable trend of inflation, particularly for non-tradable goods," said analyst Martin Amaral Neto of Banco ESSI.
"It is a signal to the markets not to get too euphoric about the prospects for lower rates," he added.
The year-on-year inflation rate picked up slightly in December to 3.3 percent, from 3.0 percent, and could tick up again during the early months of 1997 for statistical reasons, analysts say.
But longer-term it appears under control and on course to meet the government goal for an average 1997 rate of 2.5 percent, they add.
Isabel Cabral of Fincor said that after intervening to buy escudos against the mark, it would have been counter-productive for the bank to cut rates on Friday.

"The market has been discounting bigger rate cuts at the start of the year, and this may not happen. The Bank is traditionally very cautious and may not go at the rhythm that the market expected," added another analyst who asked not to be named.
The bond market was weaker in line with Spain but showed no particular reaction to the central bank's decision not to cut, traders said. Forward Rate Agreements (FRA) were also unmoved.

"Despite the stance of the Bank, the FRA did not show any great change. They anticipate that in March (short-term) rates will be at 5.55 percent against the 5.50 percent seen on Thursday," said one bank analyst.
